Chapter 5. MLflow Tracing for GenAI Application Observability

In Chapter 4, we built a tool-calling agent to answer commonly asked questions about Unity Airways. This is a relatively simple setup consisting of two components: a vector database and an LLM. But even with this simple setup, our experience when working with practitioners showed that many of them struggled to debug quality issues. They are aware of the typical pitfalls like poor document chunking, weak retrieval, or ineffective prompting. What we’ve found, though, is that the real challenge often lies in the lack of tools to help them systematically diagnose and fix these quality issues.

This is where MLflow Tracing can make a real difference. Built on open standards, MLflow Tracing captures detailed information for every step in your GenAI applications. This enables you to:

  • Check each step and behavior of an agent.

  • Pinpoint source of bugs and unexpected behavior.

  • Evaluate and improve application quality.

  • Monitor performance and optimize costs.

Tracing is becoming increasingly essential as the industry starts to build more complex agentic applications (further explored in Chapter 7) composed of multiple components, as compared to the simple example in Chapter 4.

In this chapter, we’ll cover the fundamentals of MLflow Tracing, which will be essential for observability in your GenAI applications.

Understanding MLflow Tracing

The purpose of MLflow Tracing is to provide a tool for detailed tracking and visualization of requests entering your GenAI application, capturing key information at each step as it propagates through various components, with the ultimate goal of enhancing observability. For example, in our tool-calling agent from Chapter 4, MLflow Tracing can record the input question, the query used for vector database retrieval, the retrieved information chunks, the prompt sent to the LLM, and the final response. By capturing and visualizing this information, practitioners can easily debug and understand issues that may arise in their application. Figure 5-1 illustrates this process.

While this may sound analogous to logging in conventional software application development, where application code is configured to capture logs to enhance observability, there are some nuances between the two methods. Table 5-1 describes these differences.

Table 5-1. Differences between logging and tracing
 LoggingTracing
PurposeCaptures discrete events within an application.Each trace captures the end-to-end journey of an incoming request.
ContextDoes not inherently show relationships between events.Maintains context throughout the trace, illustrating interactions at each step.
Performance monitoringMetrics such as latency are not captured directly in logs. Instead, logs need to be further processed to derive them.Automatically captures key metrics without extra configuration.

That said, logging and tracing are often used together. For instance, in GenAI applications deployed as REST API endpoints, logging captures individual events such as build progress, authentication and authorization statuses, health checks, and other operational details of the API endpoint. Tracing, on the other hand, follows the end-to-end journey of each incoming request, providing a comprehensive view of how it interacts with the different components in the application.

Before we instrument our GenAI applications with traces, let’s first review some core concepts of MLflow Tracing.

Trace

As mentioned, an MLflow Trace object captures the end-to-end journey of a request as it moves through various components in the GenAI application. In MLflow, each trace consists of two components, TraceInfo and TraceData:

TraceInfo

Captures the metadata about the overall trace, such as the MLflow Experiment ID, start time, and also any custom tags. The collected TraceInfo is useful for searching and analyzing traces later on.

TraceData

Consists of a list of Span objects containing detailed information about the individual steps. The Span objects are linked together in a hierarchical format to make it easier to understand the flow of execution in the application.

Span

A Span object captures what’s happening at each step in an application, including details like inputs, outputs, attributes, and events. MLflow comes with some built-in span types you can use to organize spans in a trace, but you can also create your own if needed. All span types work the same way with the main difference being that they help differentiate the various operations in your application.

Note

That said, the RETRIEVER span is a special span type worth calling out, as it has specific properties that are required to enable functionality in the UI and in downstream tasks. This span type is used for operations that involve retrieving data from a data store (for example, a vector database). Following the required input and output schema ensures that retrieved data is presented in a user-friendly format and can be used by MLflow for evaluation tasks. We’ll explore this in more detail later in the chapter.

We recommend reviewing MLflow’s documentation for details on what each trace or span captures, the built-in span types available, and the additional requirements for the RETRIEVER span.

In short, Trace = TraceInfo + TraceData, where TraceData contains a list of Span types. Figure 5-2 illustrates these trace components.

Instrumenting Traces

In MLflow, there are two ways to enable tracing: automated tracing and manual tracing. Table 5-2 describes the differences between the two methods.

Table 5-2. Automated tracing versus manual tracing
Tracing typeDescription
Automated tracingMLflow automatically logs traces with minimal setup. It’s the quickest way to get started.
Manual tracingYou explicitly define what to log using MLflow APIs. It gives full control and flexibility but requires more code and effort.

Automated Tracing

The easiest way to get started is by leveraging MLflow’s built-in automated tracing. At the time of writing, MLflow integrates with more than 25 popular libraries such as LangChain, LangGraph, OpenAI, and more. You can enable automated tracing by adding mlflow.<flavor>.autolog() at the start of your code, where <flavor> corresponds to the supported library. For example, to enable automated tracing for LangChain or LangGraph, you can use mlflow.langchain.autolog(), which will automatically capture the traces:

from databricks_langchain import ChatDatabricks

mlflow.langchain.autolog()

llm = ChatDatabricks(endpoint = db_resources["model_name"])
llm.invoke("How do I book a flight online with Unity Airways?")

When invoking an LLM through the databricks_langchain library, you can view the corresponding trace logged by MLflow, which captures both the input and output of the LLM call, as you can see in Figure 5-3.

The operations supported by automated tracing depend on the specific library being used. As a best practice, start with automated tracing, as it covers the standard components provided by the library. For additional components, such as custom functions outside the library or when more detailed insight into standard components is needed, supplement with manual tracing to capture what automated tracing does not cover.

Manual Tracing

MLflow provides two types of APIs for instrumenting tracings manually:

High-level Fluent APIs

Instrument tracing with simple APIs. This is easy to use with minor code modifications to your application’s code.

Low-level MLflow Client APIs

Provides fine-grained control, as compared to Fluent APIs; however, it can be more complex to implement.

Manual tracing provides fine-grained control over what is captured in your GenAI application by allowing you to define custom logic using MLflow’s APIs. In the following subsections, we explore each of these APIs in more detail. In most cases, the high-level Fluent APIs are sufficient to cover typical tracing needs.

For advanced scenarios that require explicit control, MLflow also offers low-level Client APIs. As a general guideline, use the Client APIs only when the Fluent APIs do not meet your requirements.

High-level Fluent APIs

The Fluent APIs provide a straightforward way to add tracing to your functions and code blocks. By using decorators, function wrappers, and context managers, you can easily capture detailed trace data with minimal code changes.

Let’s explore how the mlflow.trace decorator works, as shown in Example 5-1.

Example 5-1. MLflow trace decorator
#Load the required configurations
import mlflow
import yaml

with open("../conf/chapter05_conf.yml", "r") as f:
    model_config = yaml.safe_load(f)

retriever_configs = model_config.get("retriever_configs")
db_resources = model_config.get("databricks_resources")

#Create the Python class
from typing import List, Dict, Optional, Any
from databricks.vector_search.client import VectorSearchClient

from mlflow.entities import SpanType, Document


class VectorSearchWrapper:
    def __init__(self, retriever_config: Dict):
        self.vsc = VectorSearchClient()
        self.retriever_cfg = retriever_config

        # Create the index handle
        self.index = self.vsc.get_index(
            endpoint_name=retriever_config["endpoint_name"],
            index_name=retriever_config["index_name"],
        )

    @mlflow.trace(
        span_type=SpanType.RETRIEVER,
        name="single_retriever_search",
        attributes={"vs_type": "databricks_vector_search"},
    )
    def search(
        self,
        query_text: str,
        columns: Optional[List[str]] = None,
        filters: Optional[Dict[str, tuple]] = None,
        num_results: Optional[int] = None,
    ):
        mlflow.update_current_trace(
            tags={
                "vs_endpoint_name": self.retriever_cfg["endpoint_name"],
                "vs_index_name": self.retriever_cfg["index_name"],
            }
        )

        span = mlflow.get_current_active_span()
        span.set_attributes(
            {
                "filters": filters or self.retriever_cfg.get("filters", {}),
                "retriever_k": num_results or self.retriever_cfg.get("k", 5),
            }
        )

        return self.index.similarity_search(
            query_text=query_text,
            columns=columns or self.retriever_cfg.get("columns", []),
            filters=filters or self.retriever_cfg.get("filters", {}),
            num_results=num_results or self.retriever_cfg.get("k", 5),
        )

The VectorSearchWrapper class connects to a Databricks Vector Search index using the Databricks’ Vector Search Python SDK. Unlike in Chapter 4, where we used LangChain’s integration, here we intentionally use the Databricks’ Vector Search Python SDK to demonstrate the concepts of manual tracing.

Inside the class, the search method executes a similarity search on the vector search index for a given input query. It supports additional parameters such as which columns to return, metadata filters to apply, and the number of results to retrieve.

Let’s execute the search method:

client = VectorSearchWrapper(retriever_configs['retriever_1'])

# Normal search (docs don't render)
results = client.search("How do I book a flight online with Unity Airways?")

After execution, MLflow captures a trace named single_retriever_search, which can be viewed in the notebook’s UI (Figure 5-4).

For the search method, we applied the mlflow.trace() decorator, configuring the span_type to one of MLflow’s default span types (in this case, RETRIEVER), naming the trace single_retriever_search, and adding a vs_type attribute. In the notebook’s tracing UI, all of this information is reflected: the RETRIEVER span type is shown as a magnifying glass icon, the trace name matches what we defined in the decorator, and the attributes appear as specified.

We also added additional attributes using span.set_attributes(), which are displayed in the UI. Furthermore, we added trace-level tags with mlflow.update_​cur⁠rent_trace(). These tags do not appear in the notebook’s trace UI, since this UI is primarily for span-level information. However, if we navigate to the Traces tab of the MLflow Experiment UI, we can see the added trace-level tags (Figure 5-5).

The search method directly returns the results from the similarity_search method of the Python SDK. In the notebook’s tracing UI, the trace’s outputs are displayed in a JSON format, which may not be the most user-friendly to view (Figure 5-6).

This happens because, although we set the span type to RETRIEVER, the function’s output does not yet follow the schema MLflow expects for user-friendly display. Let’s fix this by adding two methods.

We’ll add a parse_search_result method that converts the output from the similarity_search method of the Python SDK into the schema (a list of mlflow.entities.Document) that MLflow expects to enable a user-friendly display of retrieved documents. Example 5-2 demonstrates this.

Example 5-2. RETRIEVER span output schema
@mlflow.trace(span_type=SpanType.PARSER, name="Parse_Search_Result")
def parse_search_result(self, search_result):
    columns = search_result["manifest"]["columns"]
    data_array = search_result.get("result").get("data_array")

    retriever_schema = self.retriever_cfg["retriever_schema"]

    mapped_result = {}
    output_list = []

    if len(data_array) > 0:
        for data in data_array:
            for column, column_value in zip(columns, data):
                mapped_result[column["name"]] = column_value

            metadata = {"score": mapped_result["score"]}
            doc = Document(
                page_content=mapped_result[retriever_schema["text_column"]],
                metadata=metadata,
                id=mapped_result[retriever_schema["primary_key"]],
            )
            output_list.append(doc)

    return output_list

The second method is the refined_search method, which functions like the original search method of the vector search index but includes an extra step to apply parse_search_result:

@mlflow.trace(span_type=SpanType.RETRIEVER)
def refined_search(
    self,
    query_text: str,
    columns: Optional[List[str]] = None,
    filters: Optional[Dict[str, tuple]] = None,
    num_results: Optional[int] = None,
    span_name: Optional[str] = None,
):
    if span_name:
         mlflow.get_current_active_span()._span.update_name(span_name)

    search_results = self.search(
        query_text=query_text,
        columns=columns,
        filters=filters,
        num_results=num_results,
    )
    parsed_results = self.parse_search_result(search_result=search_results)
    return parsed_results


VectorSearchWrapper.parse_search_result = parse_search_result
VectorSearchWrapper.refined_search = refined_search

Now when we execute the refined_search method, as follows, we can see that the outputs are rendered in a user-friendly manner (see Figure 5-7):

# Refined search (docs render)
client = VectorSearchWrapper(retriever_configs['retriever_1'])
refined_search = client.refined_search("How do I book a flight online with Unity Airways?")

In this example, we explored how to use the mlflow.trace() decorator to add custom traces. More importantly, we saw how to configure the outputs of a RETRIEVER span to ensure they are displayed in a user-friendly format.

Note

Formatting the outputs of a RETRIEVER span is about more than aesthetics or readability. The output schema of a RETRIEVER span is also required by MLflow for evaluating retrieval tasks, which we will cover in Chapter 6.

This example was relatively simple. So next, let’s explore a more complex scenario that involves parallelizing multiple retrievals and configuring custom traces for such cases. We’ll also see how manual traces can work alongside automated traces.

Let’s create a new retrieval class that takes an input, uses an LLM to paraphrase the query and generate multiple variations, and then sends these variations for parallel retrieval. Figure 5-8 illustrates this.

First, we will create a new Python class, MultiRetriever, to implement this functionality. The class accepts multiple retriever configurations and an endpoint name from the Databricks Foundation Model API. Each retriever will be initialized with the VectorSearchWrapper class that we defined previously. As for the LLM, we’ll initialize it as a ChatDatabricks object from LangChain. We also enable autologging by calling mlflow.langchain.autolog(). Example 5-3 demonstrates this.

Example 5-3. Tracing across multiple threads
# python
from typing import List, Dict, Optional, Any
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor, as_completed
import contextvars
import mlflow
from mlflow.entities import SpanType
from databricks_langchain import ChatDatabricks
import ast
import json

mlflow.langchain.autolog()


class MultiRetriever:
    def __init__(
        self,
        retriever_configs: List[Dict[str, Any]],
        llm_endpoint: str = db_resources["model_name"],
    ):
        self.retrievers = [
            VectorSearchWrapper(retriever_configs[config])
            for config in retriever_configs
        ]
        self.llm = ChatDatabricks(endpoint=llm_endpoint, temperature=0)

Next, we define a method to perform query generation. We use a simple prompt to instruct the LLM to generate multiple variations of the input query. The method returns a list containing these variations:

def query_generation(self, query_text: str) -> List[str]:
    num_queries = len(self.retrievers)

    response = self.llm.invoke(
        f"Generate {num_queries} variations of this query for vector search: "
        f"'{query_text}'. "
        "Return the generated queries as a Python list. "
        "For example: ['how are you?', 'how do you do?']"
    )

    text_items = [
        item["text"]
        for item in json.loads(response.content)
        if item.get("type") == "text"
    ]

    queries = ast.literal_eval(text_items[0])
    return queries
MultiRetriever.query_generation = query_generation
Note

Query generation is a common technique for improving retrieval recall, and it is important to monitor this step to debug any potential quality issues. Since MLflow’s automated tracing may not capture it by default, implementing manual tracing can be particularly useful.

Then, we create a method to perform parallel retrieval search with Python’s ThreadPoolExecutor. The ThreadPoolExecutor will parallelize the refined_search method that we defined in VectorSearchWrapper:

@mlflow.trace(span_type=SpanType.RETRIEVER)
def execute_parallel_search(
    self,
    queries: List[str],
    columns: Optional[List[str]] = None,
    filters: Optional[Dict[str, tuple]] = None,
    num_results: Optional[int] = None,
    refined: bool = True,
):
    combined_results: List[Any] = []

    with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=len(self.retrievers)) as executor:
        futures = {}
        for i, (retriever, query) in enumerate(zip(self.retrievers, queries)):                                                                     
            ctx = contextvars.copy_context()                                                                                                       
            search_fn = retriever.refined_search                                                                  
            futures[                                                                                                                               
                executor.submit(                                                                                                                   
                    ctx.run, search_fn, query, columns, filters, num_results,                                                                      
                    span_name=f"refined_search_{i+1}"
                )
            ] = retriever


        for future in as_completed(futures):
            retriever_results = future.result()
            if isinstance(retriever_results, list):
                combined_results.extend(retriever_results)

    return combined_results


MultiRetriever.execute_parallel_search = execute_parallel_search

Finally, we create the query_generation_search method to combine the preceding methods to execute query generation and parallel search:

def query_generation_search(
    self, query_text: str, top_k: Optional[int] = None
) -> List[Document]:
    """
    Orchestrate query generation, retrieval, and reranking, with optional top_k truncation.
    """
    with mlflow.start_span(name="Custom Retriever", span_type=SpanType.CHAIN) as span:
        span.set_inputs({"query": query_text})

        # Step 1: Generate rewritten queries
        llm_queries = self.query_generation(query_text)

        # Step 2: Run parallel retrieval
        search_results = self.execute_parallel_search(llm_queries)

        span.set_outputs(search_results)
        return search_results


MultiRetriever.query_generation_search = query_generation_search

Now when we execute the query_generation_search method, as follows, we can see that the query is first sent to ChatDatabricks for query generation and then passed to execute_parallel_search for parallel retrieval:

multi_retriever = MultiRetriever(retriever_configs)
results = multi_retriever.query_generation_search(
    query_text="How do I book a flight online with Unity Airways?"
)

The trace of execute_parallel_search includes two child spans: refined_search_1 and refined_search_2. Figure 5-9 illustrates this.

There are a few key points to unpack here. First, observe that the ChatDatabricks trace was captured even though we did not add any custom traces. This happens because we enabled mlflow.langchain.autolog(), which automatically captures traces from LangChain. From this example, we can see how automated tracing works seamlessly alongside manual tracing.

You’ll also notice that refined_search_1 and refined_search_2 are captured as child spans of execute_parallel_search. MLflow automatically detects parent-child relationships between functions, so as a developer, you can instrument traces at the function level without wracking your brains to write code to link parent-child spans.

For parallel retrieval, we use ThreadPoolExecutor. MLflow Tracing relies on Python’s built-in Context Variables mechanism to ensure thread safety, which means that, by default, traces are isolated to each thread. To create a trace that spans multiple threads, we copied the context from the main thread to each worker thread.

Note

In our Unity Airways practice example, we used the expanded queries to retrieve information from the same source. In reality, it is common to perform retrieval across multiple sources to provide richer context for an LLM. In such scenarios, instrumenting traces becomes important, as it offers visibility into each retriever’s contribution, enhances transparency and explainability of the LLM’s responses, and even enables testing of more advanced techniques, such as assigning weighted importance to each retriever.

Finally, you may have noticed that the trace for the query_generation_search method is captured even though we did not declare any mlflow.trace() decorator for this method. Instead, we used the mlflow.start_span() context manager to create the span. The difference is that the context manager is useful for capturing traces in arbitrary code blocks that aren’t wrapped in a function or when you need to trace only a specific portion of a function. The context manager gives you the flexibility to have precise control over the span placement.

Like the mlflow.trace() decorator, the context manager automatically captures parent-child relationships, exceptions, and execution time, and it works seamlessly with auto-tracing. However, when using the context manager, we need to manually provide the span details, such as the span name, inputs, and outputs.

Next, we complete this example by adding a custom reranker function. Figure 5-10 depicts this. This function leverages an LLM to determine which of the retrieved results is most relevant to the input query.

To do this, we first create a class CustomLangchainTracer. This class inherits from MlflowLangchainTracer, a handler injected into LangChain’s model inference process to log traces. Under the hood, MLflow uses this handler for automated tracing: it starts a new span for certain LangChain actions, such as on_chain_start and on_llm_start, and concludes the span when the action finishes.

If we want to customize the behavior of automated traces, we can inherit from MlflowLangchainTracer and implement our own logic. Example 5-4 demonstrates this.

Example 5-4. Customizing the behavior of automated traces
from mlflow.langchain.langchain_tracer import MlflowLangchainTracer
from langchain_core.messages import BaseMessage
from uuid import UUID


class CustomLangchainTracer(MlflowLangchainTracer):
    def on_chat_model_start(
        self,
        serialized: Dict[str, Any],
        messages: List[List[BaseMessage]],
        *,
        run_id: UUID,
        tags: Optional[List[str]] = None,
        parent_run_id: Optional[UUID] = None,
        metadata: Optional[Dict[str, Any]] = None,
        name: Optional[str] = None,
        **kwargs: Any,
    ):

        if metadata:
            kwargs.update({"reranker_metadata": metadata})

        self._start_span(
            span_name=name or self._assign_span_name(serialized, "reranker model"),
            parent_run_id=parent_run_id,
            span_type=SpanType.RERANKER,
            run_id=run_id,
            inputs=messages,
            attributes=kwargs,
        )

Next, we create the rerank_results method. This is a simple reranker that takes all the retrieved chunks and uses an LLM to determine which chunks are most relevant to the input query. When invoking the LLM via ChatDatabricks, the CustomLangchainTracer created in the previous step is passed as a callback to the invoke method. The rerank_results method returns a sorted list of the reranked chunks:

def rerank_results(
    self,
    query_text: str,
    search_results: List[Document],
) -> List[Document]:

    if not search_results:
        return []

    # Extract the text snippets
    docs = [res.page_content for res in search_results]

    # Construct the rerank prompt
    rerank_prompt = (
        f"Given the query:\n'{query_text}'\n\n"
        f"Rerank the following search results in order of relevance. "
        f"Return a JSON list of the ranking of each doc.\n\n"
        f"For example, [2, 3, 1] means: the first doc ranks 2nd, "
        f"the second doc ranks 3rd, and the third doc ranks 1st.\n\n"
        f"Search results:\n{docs}"
    )

    # Invoke the LLM
    response = self.llm.invoke(
        rerank_prompt,
        config={
            "callbacks": [CustomLangchainTracer()],
            "metadata": {"input_docs": len(docs)},
            "run_name": "CustomReranker",
        },
    )

    text_items = [
        item["text"] for item in response.content if item.get("type") == "text"
    ]

    ranking = ast.literal_eval(text_items[0])

    # Build reranked results based on ranking indices
    indexed_results = list(zip(ranking, search_results))
    indexed_results.sort(key=lambda x: x[0])
    reranked_results = [res for _, res in indexed_results]

    return reranked_results


MultiRetriever.rerank_results = rerank_results

We would also create a simple method to filter only the top-K results:

@mlflow.trace(span_type="Function")
def apply_top_k_filter(
    self, results: List[Document], top_k: Optional[int] = None
) -> List[Document]:

    if top_k is not None:
        return results[:top_k]
    return results


MultiRetriever.apply_top_k_filter = apply_top_k_filter

Finally, we update the query_generation_search method to include the reranking functionality:

def query_generation_search(
    self, query_text: str, top_k: Optional[int] = None
) -> List[Document]:
    
    with mlflow.start_span(name="Custom Retriever", span_type=SpanType.CHAIN) as span:
        span.set_inputs({"query": query_text})

        # Step 1: Generate queries
        llm_queries = self.query_generation(query_text)

        with mlflow.start_span(name="Parallel Retrieve", 
            span_type=SpanType.RETRIEVER) as child_span:

            # Step 2: Run parallel retrieval
            search_results = self.execute_parallel_search(llm_queries)

            # Step 3: Rerank results
            reranked_results = self.rerank_results(query_text, search_results)

            # Step 4: Apply top_k truncation after rerank
            final_results = self.apply_top_k_filter(reranked_results, top_k)
            child_span.set_outputs(final_results)

        span.set_outputs(final_results)
        return final_results
    

MultiRetriever.query_generation_search = query_generation_search

Now when we execute query_generation_search method, as shown here, we can see that the CustomReranker and apply_top_k_filter spans are added to the trace (see Figure 5-11):

multi_retriever = MultiRetriever(retriever_configs)
results = multi_retriever.query_generation_search(
    query_text="How do I book a flight online with Unity Airways?"
)

An interesting point is that, even though CustomReranker invokes an LLM for the reranking, its span type is actually RERANKER. This is because we modified the automated tracing behavior using CustomLangchainTracer to set the span type to RERANKER instead of the default LLM type.

Note

Reranking is one of the most commonly used techniques to improve retrieval results. Instrumenting tracing at this stage is important because it allows us to monitor the quality of the reranker, for example, whether it misordered documents and caused the LLM to generate a suboptimal response.

It also helps track performance impacts, as some rerankers can be computationally expensive and add extra latency.

With this visibility, you can more effectively experiment with different rerankers and optimize both accuracy and efficiency.

Now all that is left to complete this example is to pass the outputs of the top-K results to our LLM. We do this by creating the very simple class CustomRag. Example 5-5 demonstrates this.

Example 5-5. Output reducer
class CustomRag:
    def __init__(self, retriever, llm_endpoint: str = db_resources["model_name"]):
        self.llm = ChatDatabricks(endpoint=llm_endpoint, temperature=0)
        self.retriever = retriever

    @mlflow.trace(span_type=SpanType.CHAIN, output_reducer=lambda x: "".join(x))
    def llm_call_docs(self, query_text):
        # Extract the text snippets
        docs = self.retriever.query_generation_search(query_text)
        docs = [doc.page_content for doc in docs]

        llm_prompt = f"""You are a trusted AI assistant that helps answer questions based 
            only on the provided information. Here is some context which may or may not help 
            you answer the following question: {docs}.
        
        Answer directly, do not repeat the question. Based on this context, answer this 
            question: {query_text}.
        If you don't know the answer, just say that you don't know.
        """
        llm_stream = self.llm.stream(llm_prompt)
        for chunk in llm_stream:
            if isinstance(chunk.content, str):
                yield chunk.content

When deploying GenAI applications, streaming responses are commonly used to reduce perceived latency and enhance the user experience, especially with long answers. Let’s execute this example in streaming mode and ensure that traces capture the streamed outputs:

custom_rag = CustomRag(multi_retriever)

display_str=''
for chunk in custom_rag.llm_call_docs("How do I book a flight online with Unity Airways?"):
    display_str += chunk

display_str

In Figure 5-12, you can see that MLflow now successfully captures the output of the RAG in the trace.

In the CustomRag class, the llm_call_docs method is decorated with mlflow.trace() that includes an output_reducer. This is used to aggregate multiple elements into a single span output. You can define a custom function that takes a list of yielded elements as input and specifies how they should be aggregated. By default, if no reducer is provided, the span’s output will simply be a list of the yielded elements. Try removing the reducer logic and observe the difference for yourself.

In certain scenarios, our GenAI application may process inputs and generate outputs that include sensitive information, such as personal data. In highly regulated industries, it may be necessary to ensure that this information is not stored in trace logs. To address this requirement, MLflow can be configured to redact or mask sensitive data before it is recorded. Example 5-6 shows an example.

Example 5-6. Redacting sensitive information
import re
import mlflow
from mlflow.entities.span import Span

EMAIL_PATTERN = r"[A-Za-z0-9._%+-]+@[A-Za-z0-9.-]+\.[A-Za-z]{2,}"

def _redact(obj):
    if isinstance(obj, str):
        return re.sub(EMAIL_PATTERN, "[REDACTED]", obj)
    if isinstance(obj, dict):
        return {k: _redact(v) for k, v in obj.items()}
    if isinstance(obj, list):
        return [_redact(item) for item in obj]
    return obj

def redact_email(span: Span) -> None:
    span.set_inputs(_redact(span.inputs))
    span.set_outputs(_redact(span.outputs))

mlflow.tracing.configure(span_processors=[redact_email])

In Example 5-6, we define a simple regular expression function to match email addresses. We then configure MLflow tracing using mlflow.tracing.configure, specifying span_processors that redact any email addresses present in the trace’s inputs or outputs. This is analogous to adding post-processing hooks that will be applied to each span in a trace. In practice, this function can be customized to suit your specific requirements. When inspecting the trace, you can see that email information has been successfully redacted (Figure 5-13).

There we have it. We just built an end-to-end RAG featuring query generation, parallel retrieval, and reranking, all instrumented with manual tracing using the MLflow Fluent APIs.

Low-level MLflow Client APIs

In the previous section, we explored high-level MLflow Fluent APIs designed to make manual trace instrumentation in GenAI applications simple and convenient. In most cases, these APIs are sufficient to cover typical tracing needs.

That said, MLflow also provides a set of low-level MLflow Client APIs for advanced scenarios where you need explicit control, such as creating custom trace IDs or integrating with existing observability systems.

As a general guideline, we recommend using the Client APIs only when the Fluent APIs do not meet your requirements.

To illustrate the complexity of these APIs, we’ll extend the VectorSearchWrapper class introduced earlier in this chapter. Specifically, we’ll add a new method, low_level_search, which uses the low-level MLflow Client APIs to capture traces for the following steps:

  1. Query the vector search index using the Databricks Vector Search Python SDK.

  2. Parse the results from step 1 into the MLflow-compatible output schema using the parse_search_result method we implemented previously.

While these steps were easily handled with the high-level Fluent API in earlier sections of the chapter, achieving the same functionality with the low-level Client APIs is more involved and requires explicitly managing each step of the process (Figure 5-14).

We start by creating a trace with a root span. To create two child spans (retrieval_span and parse_span) under the root_span, we need to pass the root span’s ID as the parent_id for each child span. Because these child spans belong to the same trace, they must also use the root_span trace_id.

We also need to explicitly manage each span’s lifecycle, including when it starts and ends. For example, retrieval logic should be wrapped in a try/except block to handle failures and ensure the span is always ended correctly. This makes the code more complex.

By contrast, the high-level Fluent APIs handle span relationships, trace propagation, and lifecycle management automatically, which simplifies the implementation significantly.

Due to the complexity, the full code example is not shown here. We encourage you to explore this chapter’s notebook for a detailed walkthrough.

If you look through the notebook, it’s clear that the code is much longer and more complex compared to using the mlflow.trace() decorator. With the low-level Client APIs, you’re responsible for every detail such as starting and stopping traces and spans, managing nested parent-child relationships, coordinating spans across parallel searches, handling custom errors, and more.

While this level of control can be powerful, it adds significant overhead. That’s why, in most cases, the Fluent APIs are the recommended choice, as they simplify the overall process while still covering the majority of scenarios. The Client APIs should be used only when you truly need fine-grained control or are working with advanced scenarios that go beyond what the Fluent APIs provide. Some of these scenarios could be:

  • No automatic parent-child relationship detection

  • Manual exception handling required

  • Custom trace ID management

  • Integration with existing systems

Warning

One important point of warning is that the high-level Fluent APIs and the low-level Client APIs cannot be mixed, as they do not interoperate.

Querying Traces

We have covered in depth how to collect traces, both automatically and manually. The purpose of collecting traces is to enable observability so you can understand what went wrong and debug issues more effectively. The next step is learning how to query those traces to gain deeper insight into your application.

Head over to the Traces tab in the MLflow Experiment UI where you have an interface to run queries on your traces using the fields defined in the TraceInfo schema. You should see a screen similar to that of Figure 5-15.

MLflow also lets us query traces programmatically with the mlflow.search_traces method. This method can return results as either a Pandas DataFrame (one row per trace) or a list of Trace objects. For example, if we want to query traces that failed and had an execution time longer than 2 seconds, here’s how we could do it:

mlflow.search_traces(
    filter_string="traces.execution_time_ms > 2000 and traces.status = 'ERROR'"
)

The returned Pandas DataFrame provides you with the flexibility to further process the trace data based on your needs. Table 5-3 lists the searchable fields you can use with mlflow.search_traces, at the time of writing.

Table 5-3. Different searchable fields for traces
Field typeSearch pathOperatorsNotes
Metadatametadata.*=, !=String equality only
Tagstags.*=, !=String equality only
Statustraces.status=, !=String equality
(OK, ERROR, IN_PROGRESS)
Nametraces.name=, !=String equality only
Timestamptraces.timestamp_ms=, <, <=, >, >=Numeric comparisons (ms since epoch)
Execution timetraces.execution_time_ms=, <, <=, >, >=Numeric comparisons

The syntax rules to query the traces are as follow:

Table prefixes required

Always use attributes., tags., or metadata.

Backticks for dots

Fields with dots need backticks, e.g., tags.`mlflow.traceName`

Single quotes only

String values must use single quotes, e.g., 'value'

Case sensitive

All field names and values are case sensitive

AND only

OR operators are not supported (yes, you read that correctly)

We recommend checking the latest MLflow documentation for the most up-to-date search fields and syntax rules. The documentation also includes detailed examples on querying traces and highlights common pitfalls that practitioners often encounter.

We will not cover the specific syntax in detail, as these are details that you can find in MLflow’s documentation. Our goal here was to highlight the different ways you can access and explore traces.

In Chapter 9, we’ll take things further and show how traces are used in production monitoring for GenAI applications. We’ll walk through practical examples of analyzing traces to monitor and optimize the performance of your GenAI applications.

Conclusion and Key Takeaways

In this chapter, we demonstrated how to instrument traces in GenAI applications using MLflow Tracing. Tracing provides detailed insights into each step of a GenAI workflow, making it easier to identify the source of errors or factors contributing to poor quality.

MLflow offers native support for automated tracing with many popular open source libraries, which can also be complemented by manual tracing for more granular insights. To understand the core concepts of manual tracing, we instrumented traces for a custom RAG that performs query generation, parallel retriever search, and reranking before generating a response. As GenAI applications grow in complexity, we recommend using manual traces in tandem with automated tracing to gain deeper visibility in your applications.

Here are the key takeaways for this chapter:

  • Standard logging is not enough for GenAI applications. Unlike traditional software, GenAI workflows are complex, and standard logs often fail to provide actionable insights. Use tracing to capture the complete end-to-end journey of requests in your application.

  • MLflow Tracing consists of two main components: Trace and Span. Additionally, each Trace object consists of:

    • TraceInfo: Metadata information about the trace

    • TraceData: A list of Span objects containing detailed information about the individual steps

  • Plan on what information is important to capture. For example, you might track a retriever’s parameters so you can systematically compare performance as you iteratively tweak them.

  • Start with automated tracing, then supplement with manual traces for scenarios that automated tracing cannot cover.

  • Use MLflow Fluent APIs for manual tracing. They are simpler and more intuitive. Resort to Client APIs only when you need full control over trace instrumentation.

  • Use tags to enrich your traces. Incorporating tags provides you more options to slice and dice your traces for analysis.

Incorporating traces is a fundamental step in building GenAI applications with MLflow. In the next chapter, we will cover evaluating GenAI applications in more detail. At its core, traces are used for automated evaluation with LLM-based judges, and they are also used to capture human feedback. Later, in Chapter 9, we will explore how the traces we have instrumented can be utilized for online monitoring in production.
